newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian seeks British Queen's apology for massacre.
newsitem.headline: Indian seeks British Queen's apology for massacre.

text.p: A proposed visit by Britain's Queen Elizabeth to India has sparked demands from the nephew of an executed Indian revolutionary that she apologise for a British massacre of unarmed civilians in 1919.

"If Japan can apologise to Korea for excesses committed against Korean women who were used for the pleasure of Japanese soldiers, why should the British not for this massacre," said Jagmohan Singh, a professor at Punjab Agricultural University in the northern city of Ludhiana.
On the harvest festival of Baisakhi in April 1919, British troops opened fire on thousands of Indians gathered peacefully within a walled ground after blocking the only exit.

Indians say thousands of people died in the shooting and the ensuing stampede in Jallianwala Bagh in the city of Amritsar but official British figures say 379 were killed as they tried to flee. The massacre quickly become a symbol of colonial cruelty.
India will celebrate its 50th anniversary of freedom from British colonial rule on August 15.
The queen is due to start a visit to India around October 12, but a British High Commission spokeswoman in New Delhi said the itinerary had not been finalised.
"At the moment all we know is she will, naturally, be coming to Delhi. Other sites have not yet been decided," the spokeswoman told Reuters.
"A reconnaissance team did visit Amritsar but no decision has been taken yet on whether the Queen will or will not visit Amritsar," she said.
Amritsar, located in the agriculture-rich northern state of Punjab, is home to the Sikhs' holiest shrine, the Golden Temple.
Jagmohan Singh is the nephew of a socialist revolutionary, Bhagat Singh, who was hanged by the British for sedition in 1931.
Other Indians closely linked to the struggle for freedom say the Queen's visit itself would imply regret on the behalf of the British government.
"This demand for an apology is out of place in the present circumstances," said Vijay Chopra, whose family was involved in the anti-colonial movement. "The visit itself is an act of atonement."
